sections.heading: Maternal physiology and how it changes systemic disease
sections.html:
Pregnancy changes almost every organ system. These adaptations protect the fetus and prepare for blood loss at delivery, but they also change how chronic disease behaves and what "normal" laboratory values look like. Many Step 1 questions on systemic disease in pregnancy are really questions about this physiology.

Cardiovascular

Plasma volume rises by about 40 to 50% and red-cell mass by about 20 to 30%, so hemoglobin falls (physiologic dilutional anemia). Cardiac output rises by 30 to 50%, first through stroke volume and later through heart rate, peaking in the late second and third trimesters. Progesterone, nitric oxide and the low-resistance placenta lower systemic vascular resistance, so blood pressure falls to a nadir in the second trimester and returns toward baseline at term. In late pregnancy the supine uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, which can cause hypotension; patients are positioned with left uterine displacement. Immediately after delivery, autotransfusion from the contracted uterus and relief of caval compression raise preload again. A soft systolic flow murmur and a third heart sound can be normal; a diastolic murmur is not.

These changes explain which heart lesions decompensate. Stenotic lesions, especially mitral stenosis, tolerate pregnancy poorly: higher volume and faster heart rate (less diastolic filling time) raise left atrial pressure and cause pulmonary edema and atrial fibrillation. Regurgitant lesions are usually tolerated because the fall in systemic resistance reduces regurgitant flow. Pulmonary arterial hypertension and Eisenmenger physiology carry high maternal mortality, because the right ventricle cannot raise output and falling systemic resistance increases right-to-left shunting.

Renal and urinary

Renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate rise by about 50% early in pregnancy, so serum creatinine and urea nitrogen fall; a creatinine that would be normal outside pregnancy (around 1.0 mg/dL) may reflect kidney injury. Glycosuria can occur with normal blood glucose because filtered load exceeds tubular reabsorption. Progesterone relaxes ureteral smooth muscle, and the uterus compresses the ureters at the pelvic brim, producing physiologic hydronephrosis (right more than left) and urinary stasis that predisposes to pyelonephritis from asymptomatic bacteriuria. Renin, angiotensin and aldosterone all rise, yet pregnant people are relatively resistant to angiotensin II's pressor effect.

Respiratory

Progesterone stimulates the respiratory center, raising tidal volume and minute ventilation; the result is a chronic compensated respiratory alkalosis (PaCO2 about 30 mm Hg) that helps carbon dioxide diffuse from fetus to parent. The elevated diaphragm lowers functional residual capacity, so oxygen reserve is reduced and desaturation during apnea is faster. A PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg in a pregnant patient with asthma signals impending respiratory failure.

Endocrine and metabolic

  • Thyroid: estrogen increases hepatic synthesis and sialylation of thyroxine-binding globulin, so total T4 and T3 rise. hCG, whose alpha subunit is shared with TSH and whose beta subunit resembles TSH's, weakly stimulates the TSH receptor, so TSH falls in the first trimester. The placenta expresses type 3 deiodinase, which inactivates T4. Together these raise the levothyroxine requirement of a patient with hypothyroidism. Fetal thyroid function begins at about 10 to 12 weeks; before then the fetus relies on maternal T4.
  • Glucose: early pregnancy enhances insulin sensitivity, but from the second trimester placental hormones, chiefly human placental lactogen (with placental growth hormone, progesterone, cortisol and prolactin), cause progressive insulin resistance. This shunts glucose to the fetus, unmasks gestational diabetes and raises insulin needs in pregestational diabetes. Fasting glucose is lower than outside pregnancy, and ketosis develops quickly with fasting, which is why diabetic ketoacidosis can occur at lower glucose levels.
  • Other: cortisol-binding globulin and free cortisol rise; prolactin rises steadily; the pituitary enlarges. Alkaline phosphatase rises because the placenta makes it.
[[figure:s23f-fig120701-1]]

Hematologic and coagulation

Pregnancy is hypercoagulable, an adaptation to limit bleeding at delivery. Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII, IX and X and von Willebrand factor. Protein S falls, resistance to activated protein C develops, and placental plasminogen activator inhibitors suppress fibrinolysis. Venous stasis (progesterone-mediated venodilation and compression of the iliac veins by the uterus, especially the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery) and endothelial injury at delivery complete Virchow's triad. VTE risk is highest in the first 6 weeks after delivery. White-cell count rises, platelets fall slightly and ESR is unreliable.

Gastrointestinal and hepatic

Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle: lower esophageal sphincter tone falls (reflux), gastrointestinal transit slows (constipation) and gallbladder emptying slows while estrogen increases cholesterol saturation of bile (gallstones). The enlarging uterus displaces the appendix upward, so appendicitis pain may be above the classic site. Albumin falls by dilution, and aminotransferases and bilirubin should stay normal; abnormal values need explanation.

Immune and musculoskeletal

Maternal immunity shifts toward tolerance of the semi-allogeneic fetus: reduced cell-mediated (Th1) responses and relatively preserved humoral responses. This may explain why rheumatoid arthritis often improves during pregnancy, while SLE can flare and some infections (influenza, varicella, listeriosis, malaria) are more severe. Relaxin and estrogen loosen ligaments; fluid retention compresses the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, a common and usually self-limited problem.

Laboratory valueChange in pregnancyClinical consequence
HemoglobinFalls (dilution)Anemia diagnosed at lower thresholds by trimester
CreatinineFalls (GFR up about 50%)"Normal" nonpregnant values may mean renal impairment
PaCO2 and bicarbonateBoth fallA normal PaCO2 in an asthma flare is ominous
Total T4, TBGRiseUse free T4 and trimester-specific TSH ranges
Alkaline phosphataseRises (placental)Not a reliable marker of cholestasis
FibrinogenRisesA "normal" fibrinogen can signal consumption in abruption or hemorrhage
LeukocytesRise, especially in laborLeukocytosis alone does not prove infection

A pregnant patient's fibrinogen of 250 mg/dL looks normal by nonpregnant ranges but is low for late pregnancy, when levels are usually much higher. In postpartum hemorrhage, a falling fibrinogen predicts severe bleeding.

sections.heading: Transplacental antibodies, infections and chronic disease: mechanisms
sections.html:
IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, carried by FcRn mostly in the third trimester. This single fact links a group of maternal autoimmune diseases to transient disease in the fetus or newborn. Infections and hemoglobinopathies complete the Step 1 picture of systemic disease in pregnancy.

Maternal autoantibodies that cross the placenta

Maternal antibodyMaternal diseaseFetal or neonatal effect
TSH receptor-stimulating antibodyGraves disease, active or previously treated by surgery or radioactive iodineFetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis: tachycardia, goiter, growth restriction, advanced bone age; resolves as antibody clears over weeks to months
Anti-Ro/SSA (and anti-La/SSB)Sjogren syndrome, SLE, or no symptoms at allNeonatal lupus: congenital complete heart block from inflammation and fibrosis of the AV node (permanent), photosensitive annular rash, cytopenias, hepatitis (transient)
Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodyMyasthenia gravisTransient neonatal myasthenia: weak suck and cry, hypotonia, respiratory weakness in the first days; rarely arthrogryposis
Antiplatelet antibodyImmune thrombocytopeniaNeonatal thrombocytopenia, usually mild
Antiphospholipid antibodiesAntiphospholipid syndromeAct mostly on the placenta: thrombosis, complement activation and impaired trophoblast invasion cause loss, growth restriction and early preeclampsia

The thyroid row has a classic trap: a patient treated for Graves disease with radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy is euthyroid on levothyroxine, yet her stimulating antibodies can persist for years and still cross the placenta. Fetal heart rate and growth should be watched when antibody titers are high.

Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome

Lupus activity at conception predicts outcome. Active disease, especially lupus nephritis, raises the risk of preeclampsia, growth restriction, preterm birth and loss. Distinguishing a lupus nephritis flare from preeclampsia relies on immunology: a flare shows falling complement (C3, C4), rising anti-dsDNA and an active urine sediment with red-cell casts, while preeclampsia shows hypertension with proteinuria, often with hemolysis, raised liver enzymes and thrombocytopenia, but normal or high complement. Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I) bind phospholipid-protein complexes on endothelium, platelets and trophoblast; lupus anticoagulant paradoxically prolongs the aPTT in vitro while causing thrombosis in vivo.

Viral infections with vertical transmission

  • HIV: transmission occurs mostly around delivery and through breastfeeding; maternal plasma viral load is the strongest predictor. Suppressing it with antiretroviral therapy reduces transmission to below 1%.
  • Hepatitis B: transmission is mainly at delivery and rises with maternal HBeAg positivity and high HBV DNA. Infection acquired at birth becomes chronic in about 90% of infants, because the neonatal immune system is tolerant to the viral antigens; infection in adults becomes chronic in under 5%.
  • Hepatitis C: transmission risk is about 5%, higher with HIV coinfection and high viral load; antibody in the infant reflects maternal IgG for up to 18 months, so infants are tested with HCV RNA.

Sickle cell disease

Pregnancy increases vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, infections and VTE. Sickling in the low-oxygen intervillous space causes placental infarction, which underlies the higher rates of growth restriction, preeclampsia, preterm birth and stillbirth. Higher red-cell turnover raises folate requirements. Hydroxyurea, which raises fetal hemoglobin by inducing gamma-globin expression, is usually stopped before conception because it is teratogenic in animals.

Heart disease and diabetes: the mechanisms

Peripartum cardiomyopathy is systolic heart failure (ejection fraction below 45%) toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, without another cause. One proposed mechanism involves oxidative stress that cleaves prolactin into a 16-kDa fragment toxic to cardiac endothelium; risk factors include older age, African ancestry, multiple gestation and preeclampsia. In pregestational diabetes, hyperglycemia during organogenesis causes malformations (cardiac, neural tube, caudal regression), while later fetal hyperinsulinemia drives macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia. Nephropathy and retinopathy can progress during pregnancy, partly because rapid tightening of glucose control worsens retinopathy.

Neurologic disorders

Epilepsy usually keeps its prepregnancy pattern, but lamotrigine and levetiracetam are cleared faster because estrogen induces glucuronidation and GFR rises, so levels fall unless doses increase. Magnesium worsens myasthenia gravis because it reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, and aminoglycosides and some other drugs do the same. Migraine often improves in later pregnancy as estrogen levels stay high and stable.

The fetus "borrows" its parent's IgG for passive immunity. The same transport explains why maternal vaccination (Tdap, RSV, influenza, COVID-19) in the third trimester protects the newborn, and why some autoimmune diseases appear briefly in the infant.

Congenital heart block from anti-Ro antibodies is permanent, while the rash and cytopenias of neonatal lupus resolve as maternal IgG is cleared. The mother may have no diagnosis at all when the fetal bradycardia is found.

sections.heading: Thyroid disease, pregestational diabetes and obesity in pregnancy
sections.html:
Endocrine disease is the most common group of chronic conditions in pregnancy, and the management questions are about anticipating changes in drug needs, protecting the fetus during organogenesis and telling physiology from disease.

Hypothyroidism

  • Known hypothyroidism: levothyroxine needs rise by about 20 to 30% early in pregnancy. Increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed (a common method is two extra tablets each week), then check TSH every 4 weeks through mid-pregnancy, aiming for the lower half of the trimester-specific range (below about 2.5 mU/L when local ranges are not available). Return to the prepregnancy dose after delivery.
  • New diagnosis: overt hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4) is treated promptly, because untreated disease is linked to loss, preeclampsia, preterm birth and impaired offspring neurodevelopment. Treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism is individualized, often guided by TPO antibody status.
  • Separate levothyroxine from prenatal iron and calcium by about 4 hours.

Hyperthyroidism

FeatureGestational transient thyrotoxicosisGraves disease
TimingFirst trimester, as hCG peaks; often with hyperemesisAny time; often known before pregnancy
ExaminationNo goiter, no eye diseaseGoiter, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxedema
TSH receptor antibodiesNegativePositive
CourseResolves by about 14 to 18 weeksPersists; may improve in later pregnancy and flare postpartum
TreatmentSupportive: fluids, antiemetics, a beta-blocker briefly if symptomatic; no antithyroid drugsPropylthiouracil in the first trimester, methimazole afterward, at the lowest dose that keeps free T4 at the upper limit of normal

In Graves disease, measure TSH receptor antibodies early and again in mid-pregnancy if elevated; high titers call for fetal surveillance (heart rate, growth, goiter). Thyroidectomy in the second trimester is reserved for patients who cannot take antithyroid drugs. Radioactive iodine is contraindicated. Thyroid storm is treated as outside pregnancy, with propylthiouracil, beta-blockade, iodine given after the thionamide and glucocorticoids. Postpartum thyroiditis (often TPO antibody positive) causes a painless hyperthyroid phase at 1 to 4 months, managed with beta-blockers if needed (antithyroid drugs do not help), followed by a hypothyroid phase that may need levothyroxine.

Pregestational diabetes

  • Before conception: aim for HbA1c below 6.5% if achievable without hypoglycemia, start folic acid, review drugs (stop ACE inhibitors and statins; plan insulin), and assess retinopathy, nephropathy (urine albumin and creatinine), thyroid function in type 1 diabetes and cardiac status when indicated.
  • During pregnancy: insulin is preferred; insulin needs fall slightly in the first trimester (hypoglycemia risk) and rise steeply from the second. Glucose targets are about fasting below 95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial below 140 mg/dL and 2-hour below 120 mg/dL. Low-dose aspirin from 12 to 16 weeks lowers preeclampsia risk. A detailed anatomy scan and fetal echocardiogram look for anomalies, serial growth scans for macrosomia or restriction, and antenatal testing begins in the third trimester. Retinal examination is repeated during pregnancy.
  • Diabetic ketoacidosis can occur at glucose levels below 200 mg/dL in pregnancy and is dangerous to the fetus. Antenatal steroids and beta-agonists can precipitate hyperglycemia, so insulin is adjusted when they are given.
  • At delivery and after: delivery timing depends on control and complications (often 37 to 39 weeks). Insulin needs drop abruptly after the placenta delivers. Breastfeeding lowers glucose and insulin needs.

Obesity

A prepregnancy BMI of 30 kg/m2 or more raises the risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, VTE, stillbirth, cesarean delivery, wound infection, anesthetic complications and congenital anomalies (neural tube and cardiac), while making ultrasound harder. Management includes:

  • recommended total weight gain of about 11 to 20 lb (5 to 9 kg) for BMI 30 or more, with nutrition counseling;
  • early screening for diabetes when other risk factors are present, and repeat testing at 24 to 28 weeks if the early test is normal;
  • low-dose aspirin when obesity occurs with another moderate risk factor for preeclampsia;
  • an anesthesia consultation for severe obesity, appropriately sized equipment and weight-based thromboprophylaxis after cesarean delivery.

After bariatric surgery, conception is usually deferred for 12 to 24 months while weight stabilizes. Monitor iron, vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D and calcium. Patients who have had gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy should not have an oral glucose load (risk of dumping); glucose is assessed with home monitoring instead. Abdominal pain after gastric bypass may be internal hernia and needs urgent surgical evaluation.

A patient with hypothyroidism who has a positive pregnancy test should increase her levothyroxine the same day, without waiting for the first TSH result. Fetal brain development in the first trimester depends on maternal T4.

A suppressed TSH with mildly raised free T4 at 9 weeks in a patient with hyperemesis is usually gestational transient thyrotoxicosis. Starting antithyroid drugs exposes the embryo to their risks without benefit.

sections.heading: Chronic hypertension, heart disease and venous thromboembolism in pregnancy
sections.html:
Cardiovascular disease is now a leading cause of pregnancy-related death in the United States. The pregnancy-specific skills are to stratify risk before conception, choose drugs that are safe for the fetus and recognize when ordinary pregnancy symptoms (dyspnea, edema, palpitations) are not ordinary.

Chronic hypertension

Chronic hypertension is blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or more before pregnancy or before 20 weeks of gestation. It raises the risk of superimposed preeclampsia, growth restriction, abruption and stillbirth.

  • Baseline: creatinine, urine protein:creatinine ratio, liver enzymes, platelets and, with long-standing disease, an ECG or echocardiogram. These baselines make superimposed preeclampsia easier to recognize later.
  • Drugs: labetalol or extended-release nifedipine first line, methyldopa as an alternative; stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs and direct renin inhibitors.
  • Target: treat to keep blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg, which reduces progression to severe hypertension and preeclampsia without impairing fetal growth.
  • Prevention and surveillance: low-dose aspirin (81 mg daily from 12 to 28 weeks, ideally before 16 weeks, until delivery), serial growth ultrasounds and antenatal testing; delivery is usually planned between 37 and 39 weeks depending on control and medication need.
  • Postpartum: blood pressure often rises in the first week; check it within 72 hours to 10 days. ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are compatible with breastfeeding.

Heart disease

LesionMain risk in pregnancyManagement points
Mitral stenosisPulmonary edema and atrial fibrillation as volume and heart rate rise, often at 20 to 30 weeksBeta-blocker to slow the rate, diuretics, anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation; percutaneous balloon valvotomy for severe symptomatic disease
Severe aortic stenosisFixed output; angina, syncope, heart failureValve repair before pregnancy if symptomatic; careful hemodynamics at delivery
Regurgitant lesionsUsually toleratedTreat heart failure if present
Pulmonary arterial hypertension, Eisenmenger syndromeHigh maternal mortality, especially around delivery and postpartumPregnancy is advised against; if pregnant, counsel about termination; otherwise a specialist team
Marfan syndrome or other aortopathyAortic dissection, highest late in pregnancy and postpartumBeta-blocker; serial echocardiography; pregnancy is advised against with an aortic root above about 45 mm
Mechanical heart valveValve thrombosis and maternal bleedingHighest-risk anticoagulation problem: warfarin (lowest valve thrombosis, fetal risk dose related), LMWH with anti-Xa monitoring or a combination, decided with a specialist
Peripartum cardiomyopathyHeart failure, arrhythmia, thromboembolismStandard heart failure care adjusted to pregnancy (beta-blocker, hydralazine and nitrates, diuretics; ACE inhibitors only after delivery); anticoagulation when ejection fraction is very low; future pregnancy risky if function does not recover

Normal pregnancy causes mild dyspnea, edema and a systolic flow murmur. Features that need evaluation are dyspnea at rest or orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, a diastolic murmur, a persistent tachycardia and hypoxemia. BNP stays within the normal range in uncomplicated pregnancy and is useful in suspected heart failure.

Venous thromboembolism

Pregnancy raises VTE risk about four- to fivefold, and the postpartum weeks carry the highest daily risk. Deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy is usually left-sided and often proximal (iliofemoral).

  • Suspected DVT: compression ultrasonography of the leg. If it is negative but suspicion is high (especially for iliac thrombosis), repeat it or use Doppler of the iliac veins or MRI venography.
  • Suspected PE: D-dimer alone cannot exclude PE in pregnancy without a validated pregnancy-adapted algorithm. If there are leg symptoms, start with compression ultrasonography; a DVT justifies treatment without chest imaging. Otherwise obtain a chest radiograph, followed by a ventilation-perfusion scan if the radiograph is normal or CT pulmonary angiography if it is abnormal. Both deliver fetal radiation doses far below harmful levels. Do not delay anticoagulation while waiting for imaging when suspicion is high and bleeding risk is low.
  • Treatment: weight-based therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin, which does not cross the placenta. Warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants are avoided during pregnancy.
  • Around delivery: plan the timing of delivery; switch to unfractionated heparin near term if a short-acting option is needed; wait at least 24 hours after a therapeutic LMWH dose (12 hours after a prophylactic dose) before neuraxial anesthesia.
  • After delivery: continue anticoagulation for at least 6 weeks postpartum and for a total of at least 3 months. LMWH and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding.

Prophylaxis is guided by personal and family history of VTE and by thrombophilia: for example, a prior unprovoked or estrogen-related VTE warrants antepartum and postpartum prophylactic LMWH, while many lower-risk situations warrant postpartum prophylaxis only. Mechanical compression devices are used for all cesarean deliveries not already receiving pharmacologic prophylaxis.

Mitral stenosis often presents for the first time in pregnancy in a patient who emigrated from a region where rheumatic fever is common. New exertional dyspnea, orthopnea or atrial fibrillation in the second trimester with a diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis until proven otherwise; beta-blockade is the first step.

In pregnancy, diagnose PE or DVT before committing someone to months of anticoagulation, but start LMWH while waiting if the suspicion is strong; a delay to imaging is more dangerous than a few doses of heparin.

sections.heading: Epilepsy, asthma, hematologic and autoimmune disease in pregnancy
sections.html:
Neurologic, respiratory, hematologic and autoimmune diseases are common in people of reproductive age. Most can be managed through pregnancy with good outcomes if the disease is controlled before conception and essential drugs are continued.

Epilepsy and other neurologic disorders

  • Before conception: use the lowest effective dose of a preferred drug (lamotrigine or levetiracetam), avoid valproate if possible and start folic acid. Most patients do not change their seizure pattern in pregnancy; poor adherence and sleep deprivation are the main causes of breakthrough seizures.
  • During pregnancy: check levels of lamotrigine and levetiracetam early and then regularly (often monthly), and increase doses as clearance rises; after delivery, reduce doses over days to weeks to avoid toxicity. Seizures after 20 weeks in a patient with or without known epilepsy must be evaluated for eclampsia.
  • Labor and postpartum: continue drugs in labor; breastfeeding is encouraged with most antiseizure drugs; advise safe infant-care practices (changing the baby on the floor, not bathing the baby alone).
  • Myasthenia gravis: continue pyridostigmine and immunosuppression as needed; avoid magnesium sulfate, which can precipitate myasthenic crisis, so seizure prophylaxis for preeclampsia uses an alternative such as levetiracetam. Watch the newborn for transient neonatal myasthenia.
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome: common in the third trimester; treated with neutral wrist splints at night and usually resolves after delivery.
  • Headache red flags: a new, severe or positional headache in pregnancy or postpartum may be preeclampsia, cerebral venous thrombosis, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, stroke or post-dural-puncture headache.

Asthma

About a third of patients improve, a third stay the same and a third worsen, usually in the late second and early third trimesters. Uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous to the fetus than any asthma drug. Continue inhaled corticosteroids (budesonide has the most pregnancy data), long-acting beta agonists and short-acting rescue inhalers; montelukast can be continued in those who responded before pregnancy. Treat exacerbations as outside pregnancy (inhaled beta agonists, systemic corticosteroids, oxygen to keep saturation at 95% or more) with fetal monitoring when viable. Remember that a normal PaCO2 during an attack means fatigue and impending failure. Influenza vaccination is recommended. Carboprost is avoided for postpartum hemorrhage.

Sickle cell disease and other hematologic disorders

  • Sickle cell disease: preconception counseling and partner testing; stop hydroxyurea before conception or when pregnancy is found; folic acid supplementation; low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia prevention; vaccinations; serial growth scans; treat crises with hydration, oxygen and opioid analgesia, and look for infection and acute chest syndrome. Prophylactic transfusion is not routine but is used for selected patients. VTE prophylaxis is considered after delivery.
  • Sickle cell trait raises the risk of asymptomatic bacteriuria and urinary infection.
  • Iron deficiency is the most common anemia; oral iron first, intravenous iron when oral iron fails or late in pregnancy with significant anemia.
  • Immune thrombocytopenia versus gestational thrombocytopenia: gestational thrombocytopenia is mild (usually above about 70,000/mm3), appears late and needs no treatment; ITP may appear earlier with lower counts and is treated with corticosteroids or IVIG when counts are low before delivery or with bleeding.

Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome

  • Plan conception after at least 6 months of quiescent disease. Continue hydroxychloroquine, which lowers flare risk; switch mycophenolate, methotrexate and cyclophosphamide to pregnancy-compatible drugs (azathioprine, tacrolimus, low-dose prednisone) before conception.
  • Start low-dose aspirin at 12 to 16 weeks. Check baseline renal function, urine protein, complement and anti-dsDNA, and anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB.
  • With anti-Ro antibodies, monitor the fetal heart rhythm (commonly serial fetal echocardiography or heart-rate checks from about 16 to 26 weeks). Hydroxychloroquine lowers the risk of recurrent congenital heart block in those with a previously affected child.
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome with only obstetric criteria (such as recurrent early loss or a fetal death after 10 weeks): prophylactic-dose heparin with low-dose aspirin through pregnancy and prophylactic heparin for 6 weeks postpartum. Thrombotic APS: therapeutic-dose anticoagulation; patients on warfarin switch to LMWH before about 6 weeks of gestation.

Chronic kidney disease and kidney stones

Pregnancy in chronic kidney disease carries risks that rise with the creatinine and proteinuria: preeclampsia, preterm birth and accelerated loss of kidney function. Low-dose aspirin is recommended. Patients on dialysis need more frequent and longer sessions. After kidney transplant, waiting about 1 to 2 years with stable graft function and switching from mycophenolate improves outcomes. Kidney stones present with flank pain and hematuria; ultrasound is first, with MRI or low-dose CT when needed. Most pass with hydration and analgesia; obstruction with infection needs a ureteral stent or nephrostomy.

Naadi memory aid for lupus versus preeclampsia: "complement down, lupus up." Low C3 and C4, rising anti-dsDNA and red-cell casts favor a nephritis flare over preeclampsia.

Magnesium sulfate is the standard seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia, but not in myasthenia gravis, where it can cause respiratory failure.

sections.heading: Infections, surgical problems, mental health, substance use and partner violence in pregnancy
sections.html:
This section gathers the remaining systemic problems tested in pregnancy: chronic viral infections, surgical and hepatobiliary emergencies, psychiatric disorders, substance use and intimate partner violence. Many are screening questions.

HIV

  • Test for HIV at the first prenatal visit (opt-out), with repeat third-trimester testing for those at risk or in high-prevalence areas, and rapid testing in labor when status is unknown.
  • Start or continue combination antiretroviral therapy as soon as possible, regardless of CD4 count. Patients who conceive on an effective regimen continue it.
  • Check viral load regularly and at about 36 weeks. With a viral load above 1,000 copies/mL near delivery (or unknown), schedule cesarean delivery at 38 weeks and give intravenous zidovudine before surgery. With sustained suppression, vaginal delivery is appropriate and intravenous zidovudine is not needed.
  • The infant receives antiretroviral prophylaxis starting within 6 hours of birth. Breastfeeding decisions are shared, as described for the newborn.

Hepatitis B and C

  • Hepatitis B: test HBsAg in every pregnancy. For an HBsAg-positive patient, measure HBV DNA; tenofovir disoproxil from 28 to 32 weeks is recommended when HBV DNA is above 200,000 IU/mL. The infant receives vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours. Cesarean delivery is not indicated for hepatitis B, and breastfeeding is encouraged. Vaccinate susceptible pregnant patients at risk.
  • Hepatitis C: screen every pregnancy (except where prevalence is very low). Direct-acting antivirals are given after delivery and breastfeeding rather than during pregnancy outside trials. Avoid unnecessary invasive fetal procedures; breastfeeding is fine unless nipples are cracked and bleeding. Test the infant with HCV RNA at 2 to 6 months.

Surgical and hepatobiliary problems

  • Appendicitis is the most common nonobstetric surgical emergency in pregnancy. Ultrasound comes first, then MRI without contrast if ultrasound is not diagnostic. Appendectomy (usually laparoscopic) is appropriate in any trimester; delay increases perforation, which greatly raises fetal loss.
  • Biliary disease: symptomatic gallstones and cholecystitis are treated with laparoscopic cholecystectomy in any trimester when indicated; recurrence is common with nonoperative care. Gallstones are the main cause of pancreatitis in pregnancy; hypertriglyceridemia is the next.
  • Cirrhosis: pregnancy is uncommon but risky; screen for varices with endoscopy in the second trimester and treat with a nonselective beta-blocker or banding, because portal pressure rises with blood volume.
  • Nonobstetric surgery should not be withheld because of pregnancy; obstetric input guides fetal monitoring and positioning with left uterine displacement.

Psychiatric disorders

Depression and anxiety are common in pregnancy and the postpartum year, and suicide and overdose are leading causes of pregnancy-associated death. Screen for depression and anxiety in pregnancy and postpartum with a validated tool such as the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale or PHQ-9, and refer people at increased risk for counseling interventions. Continue effective medicines when the benefit outweighs the risk; untreated depression is associated with preterm birth, low birth weight and poor self-care. Ask about bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant. People with schizophrenia should continue antipsychotics, with glucose monitoring because some agents raise diabetes risk.

Substance use

  • Ask every patient about alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, opioids and stimulants at the first visit and during pregnancy, using a validated screening tool. Advise abstinence from alcohol; no safe level is known.
  • Opioid use disorder: offer buprenorphine (alone or with naloxone) or methadone, with behavioral support. Provide naloxone for overdose reversal, test for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and plan for neonatal opioid withdrawal care with rooming-in.
  • Stimulants: cocaine and methamphetamine increase abruption, growth restriction and preterm birth; there is no pharmacotherapy specific to pregnancy, and contingency management and counseling are used.
  • Toxicology testing needs consent and a clinical reason; reporting duties differ by state, and punitive approaches deter people from prenatal care.

Intimate partner violence

Intimate partner violence often begins or escalates in pregnancy, and homicide is a leading cause of pregnancy-associated death. The USPSTF recommends screening women of reproductive age, including during pregnancy, and referring those who screen positive to ongoing support services. Ask privately, without the partner or family members present and using a professional interpreter rather than a relative, at the first visit, each trimester and postpartum. Warning signs include delayed prenatal care, missed visits, injuries inconsistent with the history (especially to the breasts, abdomen and genitals), a partner who answers for the patient or will not leave the room, depression, substance use and unintended pregnancy. A positive screen leads to a safety assessment, documentation, safety planning and referral to advocacy services; respect the patient's choices about next steps.

ConditionKey pregnancy-specific action
HIV with detectable viral load near deliveryCesarean at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine
Hepatitis B with high viral loadTenofovir from 28 to 32 weeks; infant vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours
Hepatitis CScreen every pregnancy; treat after delivery
AppendicitisUltrasound then MRI; appendectomy in any trimester
Opioid use disorderBuprenorphine or methadone, not supervised withdrawal
Intimate partner violenceScreen privately; refer to support services

Never ask about intimate partner violence with the partner in the room, even if the partner seems supportive. Find a reason to see the patient alone, such as the urine sample or a routine part of the visit.

figures.caption: Figure. Schematic of hCG and TSH across pregnancy: TSH reaches its lowest level when hCG peaks at about 10 to 12 weeks (original schematic; not to scale).

sets.title: Leg swelling and dyspnea at 30 weeks

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation has routine laboratory studies. Her serum creatinine is 0.5 mg/dL and urea nitrogen 7 mg/dL; before pregnancy her creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows trace glucose with a plasma glucose of 84 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Increased renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate
Increased tubular secretion of creatinine induced by progesterone
Reduced muscle mass from pregnancy-related catabolism
Dilution of serum by a fall in plasma oncotic pressure only
Inhibition of the proximal tubule sodium-glucose cotransporter by estrogen
items.explanationHtml:
Renal plasma flow and GFR rise by about 50% early in pregnancy, driven by vasodilation (relaxin, nitric oxide) and increased plasma volume. Creatinine and urea nitrogen therefore fall, and a creatinine near 1.0 mg/dL, normal outside pregnancy, may indicate renal impairment. The higher filtered glucose load can exceed tubular reabsorptive capacity, so mild glycosuria appears with normal blood glucose.

Takeaway: GFR rises by about 50% in pregnancy, lowering creatinine and causing benign glycosuria.

whyNot.B: Creatinine secretion is not meaningfully increased by progesterone; the fall reflects filtration.
whyNot.C: Muscle mass does not fall in normal pregnancy, and this would not explain glycosuria.
whyNot.D: Hemodilution contributes little to creatinine changes compared with the rise in filtration, and does not explain glycosuria.
whyNot.E: Estrogen does not inhibit SGLT2; glycosuria reflects increased filtered load.

items.objective: Explain the fall in creatinine and benign glycosuria of pregnancy by increased GFR.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation with twins has had severe nausea and vomiting for 3 weeks with a 4-kg weight loss. Pulse is 104/min. She has no goiter or eye findings. TSH is 0.05 μU/mL (0.05 mU/L), and free T4 is 2.1 ng/dL (27 pmol/L). TSH receptor antibodies are negative. Which of the following best explains her thyroid findings?
options: Autoantibodies stimulating the TSH receptor
Stimulation of the TSH receptor by a placental glycoprotein hormone
Release of preformed hormone from lymphocytic thyroid inflammation
Estrogen-induced increase in thyroxine-binding globulin
Autonomous hormone production by a thyroid nodule
items.explanationHtml:
Human chorionic gonadotropin shares its alpha subunit with TSH, and its beta subunit is similar enough to activate the TSH receptor weakly. hCG peaks at about 10 to 12 weeks, and levels are higher with twins, hyperemesis and molar pregnancy. The result is gestational transient thyrotoxicosis: suppressed TSH and mildly raised free T4 without goiter, eye disease or TSH receptor antibodies. It resolves as hCG falls, usually by 14 to 18 weeks, and does not need antithyroid drugs.

Takeaway: High hCG stimulates the TSH receptor in the first trimester and can cause transient thyrotoxicosis, especially with hyperemesis or twins.

whyNot.A: Stimulating TSH receptor antibodies define Graves disease; her antibody test is negative and she has no goiter or eye disease.
whyNot.C: Painless thyroiditis releases preformed hormone, but it typically occurs postpartum and is unrelated to hyperemesis.
whyNot.D: Higher thyroxine-binding globulin raises total T4 but not free T4, and does not suppress TSH.
whyNot.E: A toxic nodule would usually be palpable and would not track with hCG.

items.objective: Explain gestational transient thyrotoxicosis by hCG stimulation of the TSH receptor.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis has taken a stable dose of levothyroxine for 3 years with a TSH of 1.4 μU/mL (1.4 mU/L). At 9 weeks' gestation her TSH is 4.6 μU/mL (4.6 mU/L) and free T4 is at the low end of normal. She has taken every dose. Which of the following changes is the major reason her requirement has increased?
options: Reduced intestinal absorption of levothyroxine due to progesterone
Estrogen-induced increase in thyroxine-binding globulin
Increased renal excretion of free thyroxine
Inhibition of peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion by hCG
Placental transfer of most maternal thyroxine to the fetus
items.explanationHtml:
Estrogen increases hepatic production and sialylation of thyroxine-binding globulin, which binds more T4 and lowers the free fraction. A healthy thyroid compensates by making more hormone; a patient taking a fixed dose of levothyroxine cannot. The larger volume of distribution and placental type 3 deiodinase, which inactivates T4, add to the requirement. Doses typically need to rise by about 20 to 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

Takeaway: Pregnancy raises levothyroxine needs mainly because estrogen increases thyroxine-binding globulin.

whyNot.A: Progesterone does not meaningfully reduce levothyroxine absorption; iron and calcium in prenatal vitamins can, if taken together.
whyNot.C: Free thyroxine is not substantially excreted by the kidney.
whyNot.D: hCG weakly stimulates the TSH receptor; it does not inhibit deiodination of T4 to T3.
whyNot.E: The fetus receives a small, though important, fraction of maternal T4; transfer does not consume most of the dose.

items.objective: Attribute increased levothyroxine requirement in pregnancy to estrogen-induced TBG.

items.stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy has irritability, poor weight gain, a heart rate of 196/min and a small goiter. His mother had Graves disease treated with radioactive iodine 4 years ago and has since taken levothyroxine; her TSH was normal throughout pregnancy. Which of the following best explains the infant's findings?
options: Transplacental passage of maternal levothyroxine
Transplacental passage of maternal IgG that stimulates the TSH receptor
Fetal exposure to radioactive iodine stored in maternal tissues
A germline activating mutation of the TSH receptor inherited from his mother
Excess iodine in breast milk
items.explanationHtml:
After radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy for Graves disease, a patient can be euthyroid on levothyroxine while still making TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies. These IgG antibodies cross the placenta, mainly in the third trimester, and stimulate the fetal thyroid, causing fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis with tachycardia, goiter and poor growth. The condition resolves over weeks to months as maternal IgG is cleared, but it may need treatment. Patients with a history of Graves disease should have TSH receptor antibodies measured in pregnancy whatever their current thyroid status.

Takeaway: Neonatal Graves disease results from transplacental stimulating IgG, which can persist after the mother's thyroid has been ablated.

whyNot.A: Little maternal T4 reaches the fetus late in pregnancy, and replacement doses do not cause neonatal thyrotoxicosis.
whyNot.C: Radioactive iodine has a half-life of about 8 days and is cleared long before a pregnancy 4 years later.
whyNot.D: Germline activating TSH receptor mutations are rare, and the history points clearly to maternal antibodies.
whyNot.E: Excess iodine typically suppresses thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) rather than causing goiter with thyrotoxicosis in 3 days.

items.objective: Explain neonatal thyrotoxicosis from transplacental TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman at 22 weeks' gestation has a fetal heart rate of 58/min on a routine visit. Fetal echocardiography shows complete atrioventricular dissociation with a structurally normal heart. She has had dry eyes and dry mouth for 2 years but no other symptoms. Which of the following maternal antibodies is most likely responsible?
options: Anti-double-stranded DNA
Anti-Ro/SSA
Anti-Smith
Anti-centromere
Anti-Jo-1
items.explanationHtml:
Anti-Ro/SSA (often with anti-La/SSB) IgG crosses the placenta from about 16 weeks and binds antigens in the developing fetal conduction system, causing inflammation and fibrosis of the atrioventricular node. The result is congenital heart block, which is permanent and may need pacing after birth. Other features of neonatal lupus (annular photosensitive rash, cytopenias, hepatitis) are transient. Her sicca symptoms suggest Sjogren syndrome, but many mothers have no diagnosis when the fetal bradycardia is found.

Takeaway: Fetal complete heart block in a structurally normal heart points to maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies.

whyNot.A: Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE and tracks nephritis activity but does not cause congenital heart block.
whyNot.C: Anti-Smith is specific for SLE but is not linked to neonatal lupus heart block.
whyNot.D: Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
whyNot.E: Anti-Jo-1 is associated with inflammatory myopathy and interstitial lung disease.

items.objective: Link congenital heart block to maternal anti-Ro/SSA antibodies.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation has a swollen, tender left calf, and compression ultrasonography shows a thrombus in the left femoral vein. She has no personal or family history of thrombosis and has not been immobilized. Which of the following hemostatic changes of normal pregnancy contributes to her risk?
options: Increased levels of fibrinogen and factor VIII with decreased protein S
Decreased levels of factor VII and factor X
Increased levels of antithrombin and protein C
Increased fibrinolytic activity from placental plasminogen activator
Decreased von Willebrand factor and platelet adhesion
items.explanationHtml:
Normal pregnancy is hypercoagulable. Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII, IX and X and von Willebrand factor; free protein S falls, acquired resistance to activated protein C develops and placental plasminogen activator inhibitor reduces fibrinolysis. Venous stasis from progesterone-related venodilation and compression of the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery explain why pregnancy DVT is usually left-sided.

Takeaway: Pregnancy raises procoagulant factors, lowers protein S and suppresses fibrinolysis, which with stasis explains its VTE risk.

whyNot.B: Factors VII and X rise, not fall, in pregnancy.
whyNot.C: Antithrombin and protein C stay roughly unchanged; increases would protect against thrombosis.
whyNot.D: Fibrinolysis is suppressed in pregnancy by placental plasminogen activator inhibitors.
whyNot.E: Von Willebrand factor rises in pregnancy, which is why mild von Willebrand disease often improves.

items.objective: Identify the hemostatic changes that make pregnancy hypercoagulable.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman who moved to the United States from a region with a high prevalence of rheumatic heart disease is at 26 weeks' gestation and has progressive dyspnea, orthopnea and a cough with blood-streaked sputum. Pulse is 112/min and irregular. There is a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex after an opening snap, and crackles at both lung bases. Which of the following physiologic changes of pregnancy most directly worsened her condition?
options: Fall in systemic vascular resistance reducing afterload
Increased blood volume and heart rate raising the transmitral gradient and left atrial pressure
Increase in plasma oncotic pressure
Decrease in cardiac output in the second trimester
Increase in pulmonary vascular compliance
items.explanationHtml:
She has rheumatic mitral stenosis decompensating in pregnancy. Flow across a narrowed mitral valve depends on diastolic filling time. Pregnancy increases blood volume and cardiac output and raises heart rate, which shortens diastole; both increase the transmitral gradient and left atrial pressure, causing pulmonary venous congestion, edema and hemoptysis. Left atrial enlargement predisposes to atrial fibrillation, which removes the atrial contribution and shortens diastole further. Beta-blockers slow the rate and lengthen diastolic filling.

Takeaway: Mitral stenosis decompensates in pregnancy because higher volume and heart rate raise left atrial pressure; slow the heart rate.

whyNot.A: Lower afterload helps regurgitant lesions and does not worsen mitral stenosis.
whyNot.C: Plasma oncotic pressure falls, not rises, in pregnancy, and a rise would protect against edema.
whyNot.D: Cardiac output rises in the second trimester; the increase is part of the problem.
whyNot.E: Pulmonary vascular compliance changes are not the mechanism of decompensation in mitral stenosis.

items.objective: Explain why mitral stenosis decompensates in pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus has needed progressively more insulin since 20 weeks' gestation; at 34 weeks her total daily dose is nearly double her prepregnancy dose. Within hours of delivery her insulin requirement falls to below her prepregnancy dose. Which of the following hormones most directly accounts for her increased insulin requirement during pregnancy?
options: Human placental lactogen
Human chorionic gonadotropin
Relaxin
Oxytocin
Inhibin A
items.explanationHtml:
Human placental lactogen (human chorionic somatomammotropin) rises with placental mass through the second and third trimesters. It has growth hormone-like and prolactin-like actions: it increases maternal lipolysis and causes insulin resistance, sparing glucose and amino acids for the fetus. Placental growth hormone, progesterone, cortisol and prolactin add to the effect. When the placenta is delivered, these hormones disappear quickly, so insulin requirements drop abruptly and hypoglycemia is a risk unless doses are reduced.

Takeaway: Placental hormones, especially human placental lactogen, cause insulin resistance that peaks late in pregnancy and vanishes after delivery.

whyNot.B: hCG peaks in the first trimester, when insulin sensitivity is actually normal or increased.
whyNot.C: Relaxin softens connective tissue and contributes to renal vasodilation; it is not a major insulin antagonist.
whyNot.D: Oxytocin controls uterine contraction and milk ejection, not insulin sensitivity.
whyNot.E: Inhibin A regulates FSH and is a marker in prenatal screening, not a cause of insulin resistance.

items.objective: Identify human placental lactogen as the main driver of insulin resistance in pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism calls the office because a home pregnancy test is positive; her last menstrual period was 5 weeks ago. She takes levothyroxine 100 mcg daily, and her TSH 4 months ago was 1.8 μU/mL (1.8 mU/L). She feels well. Her first prenatal visit is in 2 weeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation now?
options: Continue the current dose and check TSH at the first visit
Increase levothyroxine by about 25 to 30% now and check TSH in about 4 weeks
Switch to liothyronine for the rest of pregnancy
Stop levothyroxine until the fetal thyroid begins functioning
Decrease the dose because hCG will stimulate her thyroid
items.explanationHtml:
Levothyroxine requirements rise early in pregnancy, mostly because estrogen increases thyroxine-binding globulin, and the embryo depends entirely on maternal T4 until the fetal thyroid begins working at about 10 to 12 weeks. A patient with known hypothyroidism should increase the dose by about 20 to 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed (for example, two extra tablets each week), then check TSH every 4 weeks through mid-pregnancy and adjust to keep it in the lower half of the trimester-specific range.

Takeaway: Increase levothyroxine by about 25 to 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, then follow TSH every 4 weeks.

whyNot.A: Waiting for laboratory results delays the increase during the weeks when embryonic brain development depends on maternal T4.
whyNot.C: Liothyronine crosses the placenta poorly and does not provide the T4 the fetal brain needs.
whyNot.D: Stopping treatment would cause maternal hypothyroidism and deprive the embryo of T4.
whyNot.E: An athyreotic or failing thyroid cannot respond to hCG, and requirements rise rather than fall.

items.objective: Increase levothyroxine as soon as pregnancy is confirmed in a patient with hypothyroidism.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation is admitted with persistent vomiting, ketonuria and a 5% weight loss. Pulse is 108/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. She has no goiter, tremor or eye findings and no history of thyroid disease. TSH is 0.08 μU/mL (0.08 mU/L), and free T4 is 2.0 ng/dL (26 pmol/L). TSH receptor antibodies are negative. Ultrasound shows a single viable intrauterine pregnancy. In addition to intravenous fluids and antiemetics, which of the following is the most appropriate management of her thyroid findings?
options: Methimazole
Propylthiouracil
Radioactive iodine uptake scan
Repeat thyroid function tests after the first trimester, without antithyroid treatment
Total thyroidectomy in the second trimester
items.explanationHtml:
A suppressed TSH and mildly raised free T4 at 9 weeks in a patient with hyperemesis, no goiter or ophthalmopathy and negative TSH receptor antibodies is gestational transient thyrotoxicosis, caused by high hCG stimulating the TSH receptor. It resolves as hCG falls, usually by 14 to 18 weeks. Treatment is supportive (fluids, antiemetics, a brief beta-blocker if symptoms are marked), and thyroid tests are repeated later. Antithyroid drugs are not indicated and expose the embryo to their risks.

Takeaway: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis needs supportive care and repeat testing, not antithyroid drugs.

whyNot.A: Methimazole is not indicated, and first-trimester exposure is associated with aplasia cutis and choanal or esophageal atresia.
whyNot.B: Propylthiouracil is the first-trimester drug for Graves disease, which this is not; it carries a risk of hepatotoxicity.
whyNot.C: Radioactive iodine studies are contraindicated in pregnancy.
whyNot.E: Thyroidectomy is reserved for Graves disease that cannot be treated with drugs; this condition resolves on its own.

items.objective: Manage gestational transient thyrotoxicosis supportively without antithyroid drugs.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 30 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of left leg swelling and pain and 1 day of mild shortness of breath on exertion. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 98/min, respirations 20/min, blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The left calf is 3 cm larger than the right and tender along the medial thigh. Lungs are clear. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
options: D-dimer measurement
Compression ultrasonography of the left leg
CT pulmonary angiography
Ventilation-perfusion scan
Contrast venography of the left leg
items.explanationHtml:
She has signs of a left-leg DVT with mild dyspnea that could reflect pulmonary embolism. In a pregnant patient with leg symptoms, the first test is compression ultrasonography of the leg. If it shows DVT, anticoagulation is indicated, and chest imaging is unnecessary because treatment of DVT and stable PE is the same. If it is negative, chest radiography followed by a ventilation-perfusion scan or CT angiography evaluates PE. A D-dimer is physiologically raised in pregnancy and, outside a validated pregnancy-adapted algorithm, cannot rule out VTE.

Takeaway: Suspected VTE in pregnancy with leg symptoms: start with compression ultrasonography; a DVT allows treatment without chest imaging.

whyNot.A: D-dimer rises through normal pregnancy, so a positive result is expected and a negative one is not reliable without a pregnancy-adapted algorithm.
whyNot.C: CT angiography exposes the breast to radiation and is unnecessary if a leg DVT can be shown first.
whyNot.D: A V/Q scan is used when leg ultrasound is negative and the chest radiograph is normal; it is not the first test with leg symptoms.
whyNot.E: Contrast venography is invasive and rarely used; ultrasonography has replaced it.

items.objective: Begin evaluation of suspected VTE in pregnancy with compression ultrasonography when leg symptoms are present.

items.stemHtml: Compression ultrasonography shows a noncompressible left common femoral vein with thrombus extending into the popliteal vein. She weighs 82 kg. Hemoglobin is 11.4 g/dL, platelet count 236,000/mm3, and creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3
Weight-based therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin
Apixaban
Inferior vena cava filter placement
Aspirin and compression stockings
items.explanationHtml:
Proximal DVT in pregnancy is treated with therapeutic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin, adjusted for weight. LMWH does not cross the placenta, has predictable dosing and has lower rates of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and osteoporosis than unfractionated heparin. Anti-Xa monitoring is used selectively, such as at extremes of weight or with renal impairment. A platelet count is checked, and the patient is taught self-injection and given a delivery plan.

Takeaway: Treat VTE in pregnancy with therapeutic LMWH; avoid warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants.

whyNot.A: Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy and fetal hemorrhage; it is avoided in pregnancy for VTE.
whyNot.C: Direct oral anticoagulants cross the placenta and lack safety data in pregnancy.
whyNot.D: An IVC filter is reserved for patients with a contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite it.
whyNot.E: Aspirin and stockings do not treat an established proximal DVT.

items.objective: Treat DVT in pregnancy with therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin.

items.stemHtml: She continues therapeutic enoxaparin twice daily without complications. At 39 weeks she has a vaginal delivery with epidural analgesia, after her enoxaparin was held at the planned time beforehand. Twelve hours after delivery she has no excess bleeding and wants to breastfeed. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for anticoagulation after delivery?
options: Stop anticoagulation at discharge because the pregnancy is over
Continue anticoagulation for at least 6 weeks postpartum, for at least 3 months of treatment in total
Continue anticoagulation for exactly 7 days postpartum
Switch to apixaban and stop breastfeeding
Continue anticoagulation for life
items.explanationHtml:
The risk of VTE is highest in the first weeks after delivery. After a pregnancy-associated VTE, anticoagulation should continue for at least 6 weeks postpartum and for a minimum total of 3 months from diagnosis. She started treatment at 30 weeks, so 6 weeks postpartum also completes more than 3 months. LMWH and warfarin are both compatible with breastfeeding; warfarin needs overlap until the INR is therapeutic. She should not use estrogen-containing contraception and should receive prophylaxis in future pregnancies.

Takeaway: After VTE in pregnancy, anticoagulate for at least 6 weeks postpartum and at least 3 months in total; LMWH and warfarin are safe in breastfeeding.

whyNot.A: Stopping at discharge leaves her unprotected during the highest-risk period.
whyNot.C: Seven days is too short after a treated DVT and does not cover the postpartum risk window.
whyNot.D: Direct oral anticoagulants are not recommended during breastfeeding because of limited data, and stopping breastfeeding is unnecessary.
whyNot.E: A first VTE provoked by pregnancy does not usually need lifelong anticoagulation.

items.objective: Plan postpartum anticoagulation duration after VTE in pregnancy.

items.stemHtml:
A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus and a history of class IV lupus nephritis, in remission for 2 years on hydroxychloroquine and azathioprine, is at 24 weeks' gestation. She has new ankle edema and joint pain. Blood pressure is 142/88 mm Hg; it was 112/70 mm Hg at 12 weeks. She has no headache or visual symptoms.

Test12 weeksToday
Creatinine0.5 mg/dL0.9 mg/dL
Urine protein:creatinine ratio0.151.8
Urine sedimentBlandDysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts
C3110 mg/dL (90-180)58 mg/dL (90-180)
Anti-dsDNALow titerHigh titer
Platelets240,000/mm3210,000/mm3
AST18 U/L20 U/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Preeclampsia without severe features
Lupus nephritis flare
Gestational hypertension
HELLP syndrome
Physiologic proteinuria of pregnancy
items.explanationHtml:
Rising proteinuria and creatinine with hypertension could suggest preeclampsia, but several findings point to a lupus nephritis flare: an active sediment with dysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts, falling C3, rising anti-dsDNA, joint symptoms and onset at 24 weeks. Preeclampsia usually has a bland sediment and normal or high complement, and its onset is more often later. The distinction matters: a flare is treated with immunosuppression compatible with pregnancy (for example, corticosteroids and adjustment of azathioprine or tacrolimus), whereas preeclampsia is managed with surveillance and timed delivery. Kidney biopsy is sometimes needed earlier in pregnancy when the picture is unclear.

Takeaway: Active urine sediment, low complement and rising anti-dsDNA favor a lupus nephritis flare over preeclampsia.

whyNot.A: Preeclampsia does not explain red-cell casts, falling complement and rising anti-dsDNA.
whyNot.C: Gestational hypertension, by definition, has no proteinuria, and it starts after 20 weeks without renal sediment changes.
whyNot.D: HELLP syndrome requires hemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets; her platelets and AST are normal.
whyNot.E: Normal pregnancy does not raise protein excretion to this level or produce red-cell casts.

items.objective: Distinguish a lupus nephritis flare from preeclampsia using sediment and serologies.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman at 6 weeks' gestation comes for her first prenatal visit. Two years ago she had a stillbirth at 24 weeks of a structurally normal fetus with a small, infarcted placenta. Lupus anticoagulant was positive then and again 12 weeks later; anticardiolipin IgG was moderately elevated both times. She has never had a thrombosis and has no features of lupus. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this pregnancy?
options: No treatment and serial ultrasonography
Low-dose aspirin alone
Low-dose aspirin and prophylactic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin
Warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3
Prednisone and intravenous immune globulin
items.explanationHtml:
She has obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome: a fetal death after 10 weeks of a morphologically normal fetus with persistently positive lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies measured 12 weeks apart, without prior thrombosis. Management is low-dose aspirin with prophylactic-dose heparin (usually LMWH) throughout pregnancy, continued for 6 weeks postpartum, with serial growth ultrasounds and antenatal testing for placental insufficiency and preeclampsia. Patients with prior thrombosis (thrombotic APS) need therapeutic-dose anticoagulation.

Takeaway: Obstetric APS without prior thrombosis: low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin in pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum.

whyNot.A: Without treatment, the risk of recurrent loss and placental complications is high.
whyNot.B: Aspirin alone is used for antibody-positive patients without criteria-defining events; she meets obstetric APS criteria.
whyNot.D: Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester and is not used for obstetric APS.
whyNot.E: Steroids and IVIG have not been shown to improve outcomes in APS and add adverse effects.

items.objective: Treat obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome with aspirin and prophylactic heparin.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with HIV infection is at 36 weeks' gestation. She was diagnosed at 24 weeks and started antiretroviral therapy, but she missed many doses because of nausea and unstable housing. Her viral load today is 4,800 copies/mL, and CD4 count is 410/mm3. Fetal growth is normal, and the fetus is cephalic. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for delivery?
options: Await spontaneous labor and allow vaginal delivery without intrapartum zidovudine
Induction of labor at 39 weeks with intrapartum intravenous zidovudine
Scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine before surgery
Scheduled cesarean delivery at 34 weeks
Vaginal delivery with artificial rupture of membranes early in labor
items.explanationHtml:
When the HIV viral load near delivery is above 1,000 copies/mL (or unknown), a scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks, before labor and membrane rupture, reduces perinatal transmission. Intravenous zidovudine is started about 3 hours before surgery. Adherence support and optimization of her regimen should continue now, and the infant needs antiretroviral prophylaxis starting within 6 hours of birth, chosen for higher-risk exposure. With sustained suppression, vaginal delivery would be appropriate.

Takeaway: HIV viral load above 1,000 copies/mL near term: scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks with IV zidovudine.

whyNot.A: Vaginal delivery without zidovudine with a detectable viral load carries a much higher transmission risk.
whyNot.B: Labor with a viral load above 1,000 copies/mL increases transmission compared with prelabor cesarean, even with intrapartum zidovudine.
whyNot.D: Delivery at 34 weeks adds the harms of prematurity without benefit; 38 weeks balances these.
whyNot.E: Early artificial rupture of membranes increases exposure of the fetus to maternal secretions and blood.

items.objective: Plan scheduled cesarean delivery with IV zidovudine for HIV with a viral load above 1,000 copies/mL near term.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation comes for her second prenatal visit with her boyfriend, who answers most questions for her. She missed her last appointment. She has a healing bruise on her upper arm that she says came from walking into a door. Her boyfriend says he needs to stay because she "gets confused about medical things." Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ask both of them together whether there is violence in the relationship
Arrange to speak with the patient alone and ask her directly about her safety at home
Report the boyfriend to the police
Document the bruise and reassess at the next routine visit
Give the boyfriend written information about anger management
items.explanationHtml:
The USPSTF recommends screening women of reproductive age, including pregnant patients, for intimate partner violence and referring those who screen positive to support services. Screening must happen in private: a controlling partner who answers for the patient, missed visits and an injury with an implausible explanation are warning signs. A routine reason to see her alone (such as collecting a urine sample) allows a direct, nonjudgmental question with a validated tool. A positive screen leads to a safety assessment, documentation, safety planning and referral, respecting her choices.

Takeaway: Screen for intimate partner violence privately, without the partner present, and refer to support services if positive.

whyNot.A: Asking in front of a possibly abusive partner puts the patient at risk and is unlikely to yield an honest answer.
whyNot.C: Police reporting of adult intimate partner violence without the patient's consent is not generally required and can increase danger; it is not the first step.
whyNot.D: Deferring the question misses a chance to help when violence often escalates in pregnancy.
whyNot.E: Addressing the partner before speaking with the patient alone may alert him and endanger her.

items.objective: Screen a pregnant patient for intimate partner violence in private.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman with focal epilepsy at 22 weeks' gestation has had two focal impaired-awareness seizures in the past week, her first seizures in 2 years. She takes lamotrigine at the same dose as before pregnancy and reports full adherence and adequate sleep. Blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg, and urine has no protein. Her lamotrigine level is 40% of the level measured before conception. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Switch lamotrigine to valproate
Increase the lamotrigine dose and recheck the level
Add phenytoin to lamotrigine
Start magnesium sulfate infusion
Continue the current dose and reassure her
items.explanationHtml:
Lamotrigine clearance increases markedly in pregnancy, mostly because estrogen induces its glucuronidation, so levels often fall by half or more and breakthrough seizures follow. Her normal blood pressure and lack of proteinuria make eclampsia unlikely. The best step is to raise the lamotrigine dose and follow levels (often monthly) toward her preconception target. After delivery, clearance falls back within weeks, so the dose must be reduced to avoid toxicity such as dizziness, diplopia and ataxia.

Takeaway: Breakthrough seizures on lamotrigine in pregnancy usually reflect falling levels; increase the dose and monitor, then taper after delivery.

whyNot.A: Valproate is the most teratogenic antiseizure drug and would not correct the cause.
whyNot.C: Adding phenytoin adds teratogenic risk and drug interactions when the problem is a low lamotrigine level.
whyNot.D: Magnesium treats eclamptic seizures; she has no hypertension or proteinuria.
whyNot.E: Reassurance leaves her with a low level and risks generalized seizures and injury to her and the fetus.

items.objective: Increase lamotrigine dose for falling levels and breakthrough seizures in pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis, well controlled on pyridostigmine, is at 35 weeks' gestation. She has a persistent severe headache, and her blood pressure is 164/112 mm Hg on two readings 15 minutes apart. Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 0.9, and the platelet count is 168,000/mm3. Intravenous labetalol is started, and delivery is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent for seizure prophylaxis?
options: Magnesium sulfate at the standard dose
Magnesium sulfate at half the standard dose
Levetiracetam
Continuous intravenous diazepam
No seizure prophylaxis
items.explanationHtml:
She has preeclampsia with severe features (severe-range blood pressure and a persistent headache), which normally calls for magnesium sulfate. In myasthenia gravis, however, magnesium reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and can precipitate myasthenic crisis with respiratory failure; it is contraindicated. An alternative antiseizure drug, commonly levetiracetam, is used for prophylaxis, with delivery planning and close monitoring of respiratory function. The pediatric team should watch the newborn for transient neonatal myasthenia.

Takeaway: In myasthenia gravis, avoid magnesium sulfate; use an alternative such as levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia.

whyNot.A: Standard-dose magnesium can cause myasthenic crisis and respiratory failure.
whyNot.B: A lower dose still impairs neuromuscular transmission and does not remove the risk.
whyNot.D: A continuous benzodiazepine infusion causes sedation and respiratory depression and is not standard prophylaxis.
whyNot.E: With severe features she is at real risk of eclampsia; prophylaxis is still indicated.

items.objective: Choose an alternative to magnesium for seizure prophylaxis in a patient with myasthenia gravis.

cards.front: How much do plasma volume and red-cell mass rise in pregnancy?
cards.back: Plasma volume by about 40 to 50%, red-cell mass by about 20 to 30%, causing dilutional anemia.

cards.front: Why does serum creatinine fall in pregnancy?
cards.back: GFR rises by about 50%.

cards.front: Acid-base pattern of normal pregnancy?
cards.back: Chronic compensated respiratory alkalosis (PaCO2 about 30 mm Hg, lower bicarbonate), driven by progesterone.

cards.front: Why can hCG cause thyrotoxicosis?
cards.back: It shares the TSH alpha subunit and its beta subunit weakly activates the TSH receptor.

cards.front: Main reason levothyroxine needs rise in pregnancy?
cards.back: Estrogen increases thyroxine-binding globulin.

cards.front: Which hormone mainly causes insulin resistance in later pregnancy?
cards.back: Human placental lactogen.

cards.front: Which valve lesion decompensates most often in pregnancy, and why?
cards.back: Mitral stenosis: higher volume and heart rate raise left atrial pressure.

cards.front: Which coagulation changes make pregnancy hypercoagulable?
cards.back: More fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII, IX, X and vWF; less protein S; suppressed fibrinolysis.

cards.front: Which antibody class crosses the placenta, and how?
cards.back: IgG, by the FcRn receptor, mostly in the third trimester.

cards.front: Neonatal thyrotoxicosis in an infant whose mother had thyroid ablation for Graves: cause?
cards.back: Persistent maternal TSH receptor-stimulating IgG crossing the placenta.

cards.front: Which maternal antibody causes congenital heart block?
cards.back: Anti-Ro/SSA (often with anti-La/SSB).

cards.front: Which neonatal lupus feature is permanent?
cards.back: Complete heart block; the rash and cytopenias resolve.

cards.front: Risk that perinatal hepatitis B becomes chronic?
cards.back: About 90%.

cards.front: Why does magnesium worsen myasthenia gravis?
cards.back: It reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction.

cards.front: What should a patient with hypothyroidism do when her pregnancy test is positive?
cards.back: Increase levothyroxine by about 20 to 30% now, then check TSH every 4 weeks.

cards.front: Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis vs Graves: key test?
cards.back: TSH receptor antibodies (negative in gestational transient thyrotoxicosis).

cards.front: Antithyroid drug by trimester in Graves disease?
cards.back: Propylthiouracil in the first trimester, methimazole afterward.

cards.front: Preconception HbA1c target in pregestational diabetes?
cards.back: Below 6.5% if achievable without hypoglycemia.

cards.front: Recommended pregnancy weight gain for BMI 30 or more?
cards.back: About 11 to 20 lb (5 to 9 kg).

cards.front: Why avoid an oral glucose tolerance test after gastric bypass?
cards.back: It can cause dumping syndrome; use home glucose monitoring instead.

cards.front: Blood pressure treatment goal for chronic hypertension in pregnancy?
cards.back: Below 140/90 mm Hg.

cards.front: First test for suspected VTE in pregnancy with leg symptoms?
cards.back: Compression ultrasonography of the leg.

cards.front: Anticoagulant of choice for VTE during pregnancy?
cards.back: Weight-based therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin.

cards.front: How long to anticoagulate after VTE in pregnancy?
cards.back: At least 6 weeks postpartum and at least 3 months in total.

cards.front: Minimum interval after therapeutic LMWH before neuraxial anesthesia?
cards.back: 24 hours (12 hours after a prophylactic dose).

cards.front: Name two conditions in which pregnancy is advised against because of very high maternal risk.
cards.back: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (including Eisenmenger) and Marfan syndrome with an aortic root above about 45 mm.

cards.front: Lupus nephritis flare vs preeclampsia: three distinguishing findings?
cards.back: Active sediment (red-cell casts), low complement and rising anti-dsDNA favor a flare.

cards.front: Treatment of obstetric APS without prior thrombosis?
cards.back: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic heparin in pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum.

cards.front: Why do lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy?
cards.back: Estrogen induces its glucuronidation, raising clearance.

cards.front: Seizure prophylaxis for severe preeclampsia in myasthenia gravis?
cards.back: Avoid magnesium; use an alternative such as levetiracetam.

cards.front: Rule of thirds in asthma during pregnancy?
cards.back: About a third improve, a third stay the same and a third worsen.

cards.front: Delivery plan when HIV viral load is above 1,000 copies/mL near term?
cards.back: Scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks with IV zidovudine before surgery.

cards.front: When is tenofovir given to a pregnant patient with hepatitis B?
cards.back: From 28 to 32 weeks when HBV DNA is above 200,000 IU/mL.

cards.front: First imaging for suspected appendicitis in pregnancy?
cards.back: Ultrasound, then MRI without contrast if nondiagnostic.

cards.front: How should intimate partner violence screening be done in pregnancy?
cards.back: Privately, without the partner present, with referral to support services if positive.

cards.front: Recommended treatment for opioid use disorder in pregnancy?
cards.back: Buprenorphine or methadone with behavioral support, not supervised withdrawal.
